title: Japan's First Female PM Arrives in India Tomorrow. She's Bringing a $68 Billion Investment Playbook.
excerpt: Sanae Takaichi's inaugural visit to New Delhi for the 16th India-Japan Annual Summit will test whether two democracies can outpace China in semiconductors, rare earths, and clean energy.
body:
When Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi lands in New Delhi on Tuesday, she will become the first female leader of Japan to visit India on official bilateral business. That distinction matters less to both governments than what she is carrying: a roadmap to accelerate tens of billions of dollars in Japanese investment across sectors India urgently needs — and that China currently dominates.

The three-day visit, from July 1 to 3, centres on the 16th India-Japan Annual Summit, where Takaichi and Prime Minister Narendra Modi will hold formal talks on July 2. But behind the ceremonial handshakes and joint statements lies a calculation both sides have been making since Takaichi took office last year: in a world where supply chains are fracturing along geopolitical lines, India and Japan need each other more than ever.

## The $68 Billion Bet

At their last summit in Tokyo in August 2025, Modi and then-Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba set a target of 10 trillion yen — roughly $68 billion — in private Japanese investment in India over a decade. They finalised a 10-year roadmap covering technology, digitalisation, and rare earth elements. Takaichi, who succeeded Ishiba after winning a closely fought leadership election, has signalled she wants to accelerate that timeline, not just maintain it.

The India-Japan Economic Security Initiative, launched alongside the roadmap, identifies the sectors where urgency is greatest: semiconductors, critical minerals, telecommunications, pharmaceuticals, and clean energy. A joint declaration on economic security is expected to be a headline outcome of this week's summit, reinforcing both countries' commitment to building trusted supply chains as alternatives to China-dependent ones.

## Why Rare Earths Changed the Equation


![Prime Minister Narendra Modi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/5f/The_official_portrait_of_Shri_Narendra_Modi%2C_the_Prime_Minister_of_the_Republic_of_India.jpg)



> **"The India-Japan partnership, elevated to a "Special Strategic and Global Partnership" in 2014, now operates through more than 70 dialogue mechanisms and working groups."**



In March, Reuters reported that Japan was in advanced talks with India to explore for rare earth elements — the minerals essential for electric vehicle motors, wind turbines, fighter jets, and drones. The discussions gained urgency after China banned the export of dual-use items to 20 Japanese entities last year, effectively cutting them off from seven rare earth elements already on Beijing's control list.

India holds an estimated 6% of the world's rare earth reserves but processes almost none of them to the high-purity levels industry demands. Japan has the technology; India has the geology. The summit is expected to formalise new frameworks for joint exploration and processing, potentially including lithium, copper, and cobalt ventures in Africa.

## Semiconductors and the Supply Chain Race

Both governments are also pushing deeper into semiconductor cooperation. India's ambitious plan to build a domestic chip ecosystem — centred on fabrication plants by Tata Electronics and the Dholera Special Investment Region — dovetails with Japan's own push to rebuild its semiconductor industry at home while diversifying production across trusted partners.

Japanese chipmakers and equipment firms have been quietly expanding in India, and the summit is expected to announce fresh commitments on technology sharing, talent development, and joint investment in chip design and testing facilities.

## Clean Energy and Biogas Mobility


![New Delhi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg/3840px-Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg)


A new framework for biogas-powered mobility is expected to feature prominently, aligning with India's push to cut crude oil imports and Japan's expertise in hydrogen and alternative fuel technologies. Suzuki Motor, India's largest carmaker by volume through its Maruti Suzuki subsidiary, has already initiated biogas production projects in the country, giving the proposed collaboration a commercial anchor.

## The Strategic Backdrop

Takaichi's visit comes at a delicate geopolitical moment. Japan is managing an increasingly difficult relationship with China while trying to maintain economic ties. India is navigating its own tensions with Beijing, even as both sides have stabilised the border situation in the Himalayas. The United States, an ally of Japan and a strategic partner of India, is consumed by its own trade wars and a fragile ceasefire with Iran.

The India-Japan partnership, elevated to a "Special Strategic and Global Partnership" in 2014, now operates through more than 70 dialogue mechanisms and working groups. Defence cooperation has deepened steadily — Japan conducts regular military exercises with India and has transferred defence technology, including the US-2 amphibious aircraft under discussion for years.

For Takaichi, the visit is also personal messaging. As Japan's first female prime minister, her inaugural overseas summit with India's leader — rather than with the leaders of the US, China, or South Korea — signals where she sees Japan's strategic priorities shifting.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For the estimated 40,000 Indians living in Japan and the growing number of Japanese companies employing Indians in technology, manufacturing, and services, the summit's outcomes could reshape professional pathways. The 2025 Action Plan for Human Resource Exchange targets the mobility of more than 500,000 personnel over five years, including 50,000 skilled workers from India.

Japanese language training centres have expanded across India, and an increasing number of Indian engineers are finding roles at Japanese firms in both countries. A stronger economic partnership directly translates into more visas, more job openings, and deeper professional integration — the kind of structural change the diaspora benefits from long before trade numbers show up in official statistics.
